analysis.one_liner: Lets victims sue police for constitutional violations by ending qualified immunity.
analysis.headline: Introduced with 14 Democratic cosponsors and no Republican support, the bill has sat in the House Judiciary Committee with no hearing or vote since January 2026.
analysis.plain_summary: When a police officer violates someone's constitutional rights, the victim can sue under a federal civil rights law. But courts let officers escape these lawsuits under a judge-made shield called qualified immunity, which protects officers unless the victim can point to a past case where the exact same conduct was already ruled illegal. This bill would wipe out that defense, so an officer could not escape a lawsuit by claiming they acted in good faith or that the law wasn't clearly established. It would also, for the first time, let victims sue federal law enforcement officers under the same law.
analysis.who_benefits: People whose constitutional rights are violated by police — including federal officers for the first time. Under current law, many lose their cases without ever reaching a jury because they cannot find an earlier court decision that declared the officer's exact conduct illegal. This bill would let a case be decided on whether the conduct actually violated the Constitution, not on whether a past case happened to match it. It applies to suits already pending when the bill becomes law, not just future ones.

how_it_helps.text: The bill removes the defenses courts currently accept — that the officer acted in good faith, reasonably believed the conduct was lawful, or that the right was not 'clearly established' — so those arguments can no longer end a lawsuit before trial.
It covers suits already in court or filed after enactment, so people with pending cases are not left out.
It extends the same right to sue to victims of federal law enforcement officers acting under federal authority, who today largely cannot be sued under this law.

analysis.who_pays: Local governments, which typically pay court judgments and settlements on officers' behalf, along with the insurers that underwrite them, would bear higher payouts as more cases survive dismissal. Officers would face the risk of personal liability when their conduct violates the Constitution.

drawbacks.text: The bill removes every good-faith defense, including for an officer who reasonably believed the conduct was lawful at the time, so officers making fast decisions in uncertain situations could face lawsuits even when they acted reasonably.

Because judgments and settlements are usually paid by cities and counties rather than individual officers, taxpayers and municipal insurers would bear most of the added cost, and higher liability exposure could raise insurance premiums for local governments.

The retroactive piece — reaching suits pending on the date of enactment — changes the legal rules for cases already in court, which opponents argue is unfair to defendants who relied on the old rules.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For victims who today lose legitimate cases on technical matching rules, the benefit is real and direct. The cost falls on local government budgets and insurers, which is where accountability payments have always come from, though the bill's complete removal of good-faith protection — rather than a narrower fix — is the strongest fair objection, since it can reach officers who acted reasonably under the law as they understood it.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee has taken no action on it since.

narrative.text: Rep. Ayanna Pressley introduced the bill on January 13, 2026, joined by Reps. Ilhan Omar and Marie Gluesenkamp Perez (Ms. Simon) as original cosponsors, and it was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary.
The bill has 14 cosponsors, all Democrats, and no Republican support.
Since the January 13 referral to Judiciary, the action history shows no further steps — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Police departments, officers, and the governments and insurers that pay misconduct judgments keep the current shield that lets many lawsuits be dismissed without trial, because the bill has gone nowhere.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Police and governments keeping their shield

for.name: Rep. Ayanna Pressley
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Qualified Immunity Abolition Act of 2026 and made introductory remarks on the House floor.

for.name: Reps. Ilhan Omar and Marie Gluesenkamp Perez
for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsors when the bill was introduced.

for.name: 14 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Added their names as cosponsors after introduction.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Has not scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill in the months since its referral.

against.name: Law enforcement unions and police groups
against.what_they_did: Have long opposed ending qualified immunity, arguing officers would face ruinous personal lawsuits for split-second decisions; no such group has sponsored or supported this bill.

sides.party_line_note: All 15 sponsors and cosponsors are Democrats and there are no Republican cosponsors; the House majority party, which controls the Judiciary Committee's calendar, has taken no action on the bill.

industries.industry: Police liability insurers and municipal bond/government insurers
industries.note: More lawsuits surviving dismissal means more settlements and judgments, typically paid by local governments and their insurers. The industry's interest in limiting payouts runs against victims' ability to recover.

The bill strips the legal shield that lets officers escape suits for constitutional violations, and for the first time exposes federal officers to this kind of lawsuit. Officer and union interests in avoiding personal liability run against accountability for misconduct.
Governments would pay more in judgments and settlements, but fewer dismissed cases could also deter misconduct and the litigation costs it creates.

analysis.trajectory: With no Republican cosponsors and no action from the majority-run Judiciary Committee since referral, the bill is unlikely to get a hearing or a floor vote in this Congress, and bills at this stage with this level of support almost always expire when the session ends.
